analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 over seven years and ends lower pay for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act was introduced with 31 Senate cosponsors in 2017 but never received a vote, dying in committee when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps from its then-current level to $15 an hour over seven years, then adjusted it automatically each year with the growth in the median wage. It would also have phased out the lower subminimum wages allowed for tipped workers, newly hired workers under 20, and workers with disabilities in certified sheltered employment, eventually requiring the same minimum wage for everyone. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage and tipped workers, who would see their pay rise in scheduled steps to $15 an hour, plus workers with disabilities currently paid below the minimum under special federal certificates. Tipped workers would eventually keep all of their tips and get the full minimum wage in cash from their employer.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps to $15 an hour seven years after enactment, from $9.25 in the first year through $10.10, $11, $12, $13, $13.50, $14.25, and finally $15.

After reaching $15, the minimum wage would automatically increase each year by the growth in the median hourly wage of all employees, as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, so it would no longer lose value between congressional raises.

The bill phases out the separate lower minimum wage for tipped employees by raising their cash wage $1.15 per year until it equals the full minimum wage, after which tipped workers would be entitled to the full federal minimum from their employer plus whatever tips they receive, with a guaranteed right to retain their tips.

The bill phases out the subminimum wage for newly hired workers under age 20 and for workers with disabilities employed under Labor Department special certificates, with a schedule of increases for workers with disabilities and a prohibition on issuing new certificates, followed by a full sunset of the subminimum program.
The Department of Labor must publish each wage increase at least 60 days before it takes effect and, on request, help employers and workers with disabilities transition to the new requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with large numbers of low-wage workers, especially restaurants that rely on the tipped minimum wage, would bear higher payroll costs. Some economists and restaurant operators warn that steep increases can lead to reduced hours, automation, or higher menu prices, and disability-service providers warned that eliminating the subminimum certificate program could reduce job options for some workers with severe disabilities.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows the tipped cash wage to rise only $1.15 per year while phasing out the tip credit, which in practice raises restaurant labor costs on a fixed schedule regardless of business conditions; operators of full-service restaurants argue this falls hardest on small, low-margin establishments.

The bill sunsets the section 14(c) subminimum wage program for workers with disabilities, which disability-service providers have argued could eliminate some sheltered employment options for workers with the most significant disabilities; the bill responds with transition assistance and a requirement to help ensure continuing employment opportunities, but the risk of job loss during the transition is real.

A seven-year climb to $15 is a large jump relative to the minimum wage's historical value, and critics argue it outpaces what many regional labor markets can absorb; the automatic indexing to median wage growth then makes the floor permanent and rising.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of workers earning at or near the federal minimum wage, the scheduled raises are the largest federal pay increase this bill could deliver, and the indexing prevents the floor from eroding again. The costs are concentrated on low-wage employers, and the phase-out of the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities carries a genuine transition risk for a small, vulnerable group. The trade-off is substantial on the worker side, but the bill's rigid step schedule, including the tipped-wage timing, gives employers little flexibility.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 25, 2017, by Senator Bernie Sanders with 31 cosponsors, all Democrats.

It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and the action record shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call ever took place during the 115th Congress.
The bill never received a vote in either chamber before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the federal minimum wage, especially restaurants relying on the tipped minimum wage and providers holding subminimum wage certificates for workers with disabilities, are better off because the bill never advanced. The wage floor stayed at $7.25, where it has remained since 2009, so low-wage workers gained nothing.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Raise the Wage Act and gathered 31 Democratic cosponsors for it.

for.name: 31 Democratic senators
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of the entire Democratic conference in the Senate.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill after it was referred to his committee, leaving it with no action beyond referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Majority party in the Senate during the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the Republican majority took no floor action on it during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 supporters (Sanders plus 31 cosponsors) were Democrats or the independent Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled committee and Senate took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill phases out the tipped minimum wage and raises the cash wage to $15, sharply increasing restaurant labor costs. Restaurant operators benefit from the current system, in which the customer's tip substitutes for part of the employer's wage obligation.
Large employers of minimum-wage workers would face step increases to $15 plus automatic indexing. Workers at those employers would gain the wages employers would pay.

The bill sunsets the federal certificates that let these employers pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage. Providers lose the subminimum cost structure, while affected workers move to the full minimum wage.
Workers paid near the federal minimum would see scheduled raises to $15 and automatic indexing thereafter, the direct beneficiaries of the bill.
